title: Lying to the Spirit, Defying the Council
sum: The chapter opens with a shock. Ananias and Sapphira sell land, keep part of the price, and pretend to give it all. Peter exposes the lie as a lie to the Holy Spirit, to God himself, and both fall dead. Great fear comes on the church, which Acts names as a "church" here for the first time.

Then the scene widens. The apostles heal crowds at Solomon's Porch; the sick are laid in the streets for Peter's shadow. The high priest's party jails them, an angel lets them out, and they are found teaching in the temple at dawn. Before the Sanhedrin Peter says, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people." The council wants them dead, but the Pharisee Gamaliel warns that if this movement is from God they cannot stop it. The apostles are whipped and leave rejoicing that they were found worthy to be dishonored for the Name.
The chapter sets judgment inside the church beside persecution from outside. Below are deep dives on the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira and on Gamaliel's Theudas.
readings: Historians accept that the first believers shared goods, met in the temple, were questioned by the priestly leaders and found a defender among the Pharisees. Gamaliel is a well-known figure. The difficulties are the miraculous deaths and release, which historians cannot test, and the date of Theudas (see the deep dive).

Luke builds the chapter in two panels that mirror each other: a threat from inside (a lie) and a threat from outside (the council). In both, God acts: in judgment on the liars, in rescue for the apostles. The repeated "fear" (5:5, 11) and "the people" who admire the apostles (5:13, 26) frame a church that is both holy and popular, feared and growing.
Read as a word to the church

Christian preachers have long read Ananias and Sapphira as a warning against hypocrisy and the love of reputation, and the apostles' joy under the whip as the pattern for suffering for Christ. Chrysostom stressed that the couple's sin was not keeping money but sacrilege: taking back what they had pledged to God and lying about it.

views.H: The Sadducee high priests controlled the temple and its police, the Sanhedrin met under them, and Pharisees like Gamaliel sat in it with real influence among the people (Josephus, Antiquities 18.15–17). Flogging of up to thirty-nine lashes was a recognized disciplinary punishment. The rebels Theudas and Judas the Galilean are known from Josephus; the order and dating of Theudas is the chapter's best-known historical problem.
views.C: Many critical scholars, such as Ernst Haenchen and Richard Pervo, think Luke shaped the Ananias story as a founding legend on the model of Achan (Joshua 7), and see the prison escape as a literary motif. Gamaliel's speech, with its Theudas problem, is often cited as evidence that Luke composed the speeches. Others, such as Craig Keener, argue that Luke used reliable traditions and wrote within ancient history-writing.
views.L: Luke links the scenes by his filling words: Satan filled Ananias' heart (5:3) and the apostles have filled Jerusalem with their teaching (5:28), both with plēroō; the Spirit filled the believers (4:31) and jealousy filled the priests (5:17), both with pimplēmi. The Seven and Stephen are "full" (plērēs, 6:3, 5, 8; 7:55). Gamaliel's "torn down" (5:38–39) prepares for the charge against Stephen (6:14). The rejoicing apostles (5:41) recall Jesus' beatitude for the persecuted.
views.J: The chapter shows a debate inside Judaism. The apostles teach in the temple and appeal to "the God of our ancestors" (5:30). The Sadducees oppose them; the Pharisee Gamaliel, honored by the whole people, defends their right to be tested by time, a principle found later in the Mishnah (Avot 4:11). Jewish scholars note that Acts here presents Pharisaic leadership more favorably than the Gospels often do.
views.T: The fathers read 5:3–4 as proof of the Spirit's divinity and used Ananias and Sapphira in teaching on vows and sacrilege, and on monastic poverty. Peter's discernment was read as an example of apostolic authority. "We must obey God" became a classic text for martyrs before pagan judges.

deep.b:
Readers have always found this story hard. Four questions recur:

  • What was the sin? Not keeping money: Peter says the land and the money were theirs (5:4). The sin was a lie meant to win honor, a lie told to the Holy Spirit present in the community.
  • Why so severe? Many compare Achan at the start of Israel's life in the land (Joshua 7) and Nadab and Abihu at the start of the tabernacle's worship (Leviticus 10). At the founding of a new stage, holiness is shown in a sharp way, and later the church handles sin through discipline and repentance (compare 1 Corinthians 5; 2 Corinthians 2:5–11).
  • Did Peter kill them? No. Peter pronounces no curse on Ananias; he only exposes the lie. With Sapphira he foretells what happens. Luke presents the deaths as God's act.
  • Were they lost? Luke does not say. Many interpreters, from early preachers to modern commentators, think they were believers disciplined by death, as Paul says some at Corinth were (1 Corinthians 11:30–32).

Gamaliel speaks in the mid-30s. He names Theudas first, then "after him" Judas the Galilean "at the time of the registration" (AD 6). Josephus (Antiquities 20.97–98) describes a Theudas who claimed to be a prophet and promised to part the Jordan, and was killed by the governor Cuspius Fadus, who ruled about AD 44–46. A few lines later he mentions the sons of Judas the Galilean (20.102).

  • Two men named Theudas. Theudas was a common name, and Josephus describes many uprisings after Herod's death in 4 BC (Antiquities 17.269–285). An earlier Theudas could be one of them. Defenders of this view note that Gamaliel's four hundred men do not match Josephus' "great part of the people."
  • Luke's mistake. Luke knew of Theudas and Judas from tradition and placed them wrongly, putting into Gamaliel's mouth a rebel who rose after the speech was given.
  • Luke read Josephus. Some, such as Steve Mason and Richard Pervo, think Luke had read Josephus' Antiquities (AD 93–94) and misremembered the order because Josephus mentions Judas' sons right after Theudas. This view makes Acts a second-century or very late first-century book; most scholars think the similarities are too thin to prove Luke used Josephus.

None of these can be proved.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two kinds of filling
deep.b: Luke's filling words point in four directions in chapter 5 and just before it: Satan filled Ananias' heart (5:3) and the apostles filled Jerusalem with their teaching (5:28), both with the verb plēroō; the Spirit filled the believers (4:31) and jealousy filled the high priest's party (5:17), both with the related verb pimplēmi. Then the adjective plērēs, "full," takes over: the Seven are to be "full of the Spirit and wisdom" (6:3), and Stephen is "full" three times (6:5, 8; 7:55). My suggestion is that Luke uses this cluster of words to ask what each person is full of, and the chapters ask the reader the same question. The words are two verbs and an adjective, not one verb, so this is a reading of Luke's vocabulary, not a claim the text makes outright; commentators have noted the filling language, but I have not seen it tracked across 4:31–7:55 in this way.

echoes: Joshua 7:1–26; Leviticus 10:1–3; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Deuteronomy 25:1–3; Matthew 5:11–12; Matthew 10:17; Matthew 27:25; Luke 22:3; 4:19; 4:32–37; 12:6–11; 16:25–26; 22:3; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24

settings.when: as Ananias lays part of the price at the apostles' feet, pretending it is the whole
settings.why: to expose a lie told to the Holy Spirit, and to make plain that the gift was free and the sin was the deceit, not the keeping of money
settings.readers: Luke's churches, which had common funds and gifts, learned that the Spirit-filled community could not be fooled and that giving for show was a lie to God.

settings.when: she comes in not knowing her husband is dead
settings.why: to give her the chance to tell the truth; when she repeats the lie, Peter names it as testing the Lord's Spirit and foretells her death
settings.readers: The story warned Luke's readers that agreeing together in a lie is a shared sin, and that each person answers for it.

settings.to: the apostles, at night, outside the prison
settings.when: after the high priest's party has jailed them
settings.why: to send them straight back to the very place they were forbidden to teach, with "every word of this life"; the release is not escape but a renewed commission
settings.readers: Luke's readers, some facing arrest themselves, learned that God could open prisons, but that the point of release was to keep speaking.

settings.to: the apostles, standing before the Sanhedrin
settings.when: after they are brought back from the temple
settings.why: to accuse them of breaking the council's order (4:18) and of trying to make the leaders guilty of Jesus' death
settings.readers: Luke shows his readers that the leaders' fear was of blame for Jesus' blood, and that the apostles' answer was repentance offered to Israel, not revenge.

settings.to: the high priest and the Sanhedrin
settings.when: under questioning, at risk of death
settings.why: to justify their disobedience (God must be obeyed first), to restate the gospel in brief (God raised the Jesus you killed and made him Founder and Savior), and to offer Israel repentance and forgiveness, with the Spirit as a second witness
settings.readers: For Luke's readers this is a model defense: respectful, unbending on the main point, and still offering the accusers forgiveness.

settings.by: Gamaliel, a Pharisee teacher of the law
settings.to: the Sanhedrin, in closed session, after the apostles are taken out
settings.when: when the council is furious and wants to kill the apostles
settings.why: to stop a death sentence by reminding the council that failed movements die by themselves, and warning that a movement from God cannot be stopped and that fighting it would be fighting God
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew the outcome: the movement had lasted and spread to Rome. Gamaliel's test, given by an honored Jewish teacher, became an argument that the church was God's work.
views: Gamaliel was open to the possibility that God was at work, as the Pharisees in 23:9 are.
Gamaliel wanted to avoid an unpopular execution and a clash with the crowds; his advice is wait and see, not belief.

traditions.q: Peter says Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit and so lied to God (5:3–4). Is the Holy Spirit a person, and fully God?
views: Yes. The Holy Spirit is one of the three persons of the Trinity, of one being with the Father and the Son (Catechism 685).

Yes. The Spirit is "the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified" (Nicene Creed, 381). The Orthodox reject the Western addition that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son.
Yes. In the one God there are three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, of one substance, power and eternity (Westminster Confession 2.3).
The Spirit is God himself, the one God acting in his people, not a separate person from the Father and the Son.
No. The holy spirit is God's active force, not a person; lying to it is lying to God because it is God's own power at work.
The Holy Ghost is a distinct personage of spirit, a member of the Godhead with the Father and the Son, one with them in purpose but a separate being (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22).

title: Seven Chosen to Serve
sum: The church is growing, and growth brings strain. Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are being passed over in the daily food distribution. The Twelve call the whole community together: they will not leave the word of God to run the food service, so the community is to choose seven trusted men full of the Spirit and wisdom. The seven chosen all have Greek names, and one is a convert from Antioch. The apostles pray and lay hands on them, and the word of God keeps growing, even among the priests.

Then one of the Seven, Stephen, steps into the spotlight. He works wonders and wins debates in the Greek-speaking synagogues. His opponents cannot answer him, so they plant men to accuse him of blasphemy against Moses and God, stir up the people and the leaders, and bring him before the Sanhedrin. False witnesses say he keeps speaking against the temple and the law, and that Jesus will tear down the temple and change Moses' customs. The council stares at him, and his face looks like an angel's.
Below are deep dives on the Hellenists and on whether the Seven were the first deacons.
readings: Most historians take 6:1 seriously: the first church had two language groups, and the Greek speakers, with Stephen as a leader, may have held more radical views of the temple and the law than the Aramaic-speaking apostles. That would explain why the persecution in 8:1 scattered "everyone but the apostles."

Many churches have read 6:1–6 as the founding of the diaconate and as a model for how a church solves problems: listen to a complaint, involve the whole community, choose qualified people, pray and commission them.

Luke uses a small administrative crisis to introduce the two men who will carry the story forward, Stephen (6:8–8:2) and Philip (8:4–40). The table servers become preachers; the story's center moves from the Twelve to the Hellenists, and from Jerusalem outward.

views.H: Jerusalem had many synagogues for Jews from abroad, organized by language and origin (6:9). The Theodotus inscription shows a Greek-speaking synagogue with lodging for pilgrims. Care for widows was a known duty of Jewish communities. The scene fits what is known of a bilingual Jerusalem in the 30s.
views.C: Many critical scholars, following F. C. Baur and later Martin Hengel, see in 6:1 a sign of a deeper split: the Hellenists were a distinct group with their own leaders (the Seven), and Luke has softened a theological conflict into a dispute over food. Others think Luke's account is plausible as it stands. Whether the Seven are deacons is anachronistic for Luke, who never uses the word.
views.L: The diakonia word family (6:1, 2, 4) ties the scene together. The summary in 6:7 closes the first major section of Acts. Stephen's trial is told to echo Jesus' own: false witnesses, the temple charge (which Luke left out of Jesus' trial), the Sanhedrin, and a face shining like Moses'.
views.J: Everyone in the chapter is Jewish: Hebrews and Hellenists, the convert Nicolaus, the priests who believe, and Stephen's opponents in the synagogues of the dispersion. The dispute is about the meaning of the temple and Moses' customs within Judaism. Jewish scholars note that charges of speaking against the temple were taken seriously because the temple was the center of Jewish life, as Jeremiah's trial shows.
views.T: The fathers saw the Seven as the first deacons (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.12.10), and the laying on of hands as ordination. Liturgies for ordaining deacons in East and West read this chapter. Stephen is honored as "archdeacon and protomartyr" in the Orthodox calendar.

deep.b:
Luke never defines the word. Three views:

  • Greek-speaking Jews. The common view (Martin Hengel and most commentators): Jews from the dispersion living in Jerusalem, whose first language was Greek, as against the "Hebrews," whose first language was Aramaic. This fits 9:29, where Hellenists are Jews who want to kill Paul.
  • Jews of a Greek way of life. Some stress culture more than language: Hellenists may have been more open to Greek ways and more critical of the temple, as Stephen's speech suggests.
  • Gentiles. Henry Cadbury argued that the Hellenists were Gentiles. Few accept this now, since Acts does not show Gentiles joining the church until Cornelius (chapter 10).

Whatever the label, the complaint was handled by giving the minority group responsibility: all seven names are Greek.

deep.h: Were the Seven the first deacons?
deep.b: Acts calls them "the Seven" (21:8), never deacons, though the verb diakonein "to serve" describes their task (6:2). Irenaeus in the 180s already called Stephen the first deacon, and most Western tradition followed him. But the Council in Trullo (692) said the Seven were appointed to serve tables, not to the deacon's ministry at the altar. Many modern scholars see the Seven as leaders of the Hellenist believers, closer to elders than to later deacons, since Stephen and Philip preach, and Philip baptizes (8:12, 38). Others say the later office grew from this kind of appointment: chosen by the community, commissioned by leaders with prayer and the laying on of hands, for practical service. The Where Christians differ card below sets out how the churches read it today.

echoes: Exodus 16:7–9; Exodus 18:13–26; Exodus 34:29–35; Numbers 8:10; Numbers 11:16–17; Numbers 27:18–23; Jeremiah 26:1–24; Matthew 26:59–61; Mark 14:57–58; John 2:19; 1 Timothy 3:8–13; 8:5–40; 21:8–9

settings.to: the whole body of the disciples in Jerusalem, Hebrews and Hellenists together
settings.when: after the Hellenists complain that their widows are passed over in the daily serving
settings.why: to solve a real injustice without dividing the church, by giving the community the choice of seven trusted men while the apostles keep to prayer and the word
settings.readers: Luke's mixed churches of Jews and Gentiles saw how the first church settled a quarrel between groups: by listening, sharing responsibility and praying.

settings.by: men planted by Stephen's opponents, then false witnesses
settings.to: the people, the elders and the scribes, and then the Sanhedrin
settings.when: after Stephen's opponents from the synagogues of the dispersion lose their debates with him
settings.why: to turn a theological argument into a capital charge of blasphemy against Moses, God, the temple and the law, the same charge brought against Jesus
settings.readers: Luke's readers, whose faith was accused of abandoning Moses, saw that the charge was old, false as stated, and answered in Stephen's speech. If Acts was written after AD 70, as most scholars think, they also knew the temple had fallen; if it was written about 62, the charge about the temple still pointed to the future.

traditions.q: Were the Seven the first deacons, and what is a deacon today?
views: The diaconate is the third degree of holy orders, conferred by the bishop's laying on of hands "not unto the priesthood, but unto a ministry of service" (Lumen Gentium 29; Catechism 1569–1571). Tradition sees its origin in Acts 6. Since the Second Vatican Council, married men may be ordained permanent deacons.

Deacons are ordained clergy who serve the bishop and assist at the Divine Liturgy. Stephen is honored as archdeacon and first martyr, though the Council in Trullo (692, canon 16) held that the Seven of Acts were appointed to serve tables, not to the liturgical diaconate.

"From the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church: Bishops, Priests, and Deacons" (Preface to the Ordinal, 1662). The Ordinal reads Acts 6 at the ordering of deacons, who are ordained by a bishop and are often later ordained priests.

Deacons hold a permanent, distinct office of mercy, caring for the poor and the church's goods, chosen by the congregation; it is not a step toward the ministry of the word. Calvin built this office on Acts 6 (Institutes 4.3.9).

The church's "scriptural officers are pastors and deacons" (Baptist Faith and Message, article 6). Deacons are chosen by the congregation to serve, often modeled on the Seven; the laying on of hands is a recognition, not a sacrament.

title: Stephen's Speech and Death
sum: Asked whether the charges are true, Stephen answers with the longest speech in Acts. He retells Israel's story: God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia and promised him a land he never owned; Joseph, sold by his jealous brothers, was raised up by God in Egypt; Moses, raised in Pharaoh's court, tried to rescue his people and was pushed away, then was sent back by God as ruler and redeemer, met at a burning bush on holy ground in the desert. Israel turned to a calf and to the star gods, though they had the tent God designed. David asked to find a dwelling for God; Solomon built a house; but the Most High does not live in what hands have made.

Then the speech turns. "Stiff-necked men!" Stephen says: like their ancestors, who killed the prophets, they have betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, and they have not kept the law they received through angels. The council is enraged. Stephen, full of the Spirit, sees God's glory and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They drive him out of the city and stone him, while a young man named Saul guards their cloaks. Stephen prays for Jesus to receive his spirit and for his killers to be forgiven, and falls asleep.
The speech follows the Greek Old Testament and differs from the Hebrew in several places; the deep dive below lists them all, with the readings.
readings: Stephen answers the charges: he honors Abraham, Moses and the law ("living sayings"), and shows that God was worshiped before there was a temple and is not confined to one. The real lawbreakers, he says, are those who did not keep the law and killed the prophets.

The speech is less a defense than a prophet's indictment, in the tradition of Nehemiah 9, Psalm 106 and Ezekiel 20: a retelling of Israel's history as a story of God's faithfulness and the people's resistance. Stephen speaks as an Israelite to Israel's leaders, "our ancestors" until 7:51.
Read as the turning point of Acts

Stephen's death is the hinge of Luke's story. It ends the Jerusalem section, scatters the believers into Judea and Samaria, and introduces Saul. Luke tells it to mirror Jesus' passion, so the church's first martyr dies as his Lord did.

views.H: The speech uses the Greek Old Testament throughout, which fits a Greek-speaking Jewish speaker. Its differences from the Hebrew text (the seventy-five persons, the place of Abraham's call, the tomb at Shechem) match traditions known from the Septuagint, the Samaritan Pentateuch, Philo and Josephus. The stoning outside the city, with witnesses throwing first, follows the law's procedure, but whether there was a verdict is unclear; under Roman rule it may have been a lynching.
views.C: Most critical scholars think Luke composed the speech, as ancient historians composed speeches to fit the speaker and the occasion (Thucydides 1.22). Some, such as Martin Hengel and Marcel Simon, think it preserves the views of the Hellenist circle around Stephen, especially its criticism of the temple; Martin Scharlemann argued for Samaritan contacts. Its differences from Genesis and Exodus are evidence of the sources and traditions behind it, not simply errors.
views.L: The speech is built around rejected deliverers (Joseph, Moses, the prophets, the Righteous One) and around place: "this place" (6:13–14; 7:7), holy ground in the desert (7:33), the tent and the house (7:44–50). Luke's account of Stephen's death mirrors Jesus' death in his Gospel: the Son of Man at God's right hand (Luke 22:69), the spirit committed (Luke 23:46), the prayer for the killers (Luke 23:34).
views.J: Stephen speaks as a Jew, of "our father Abraham" and "our ancestors," using Israel's own prophetic tradition of self-criticism. Jewish scholars point out that criticism of the temple was also found in other Jewish groups, such as the Qumran community, and that the speech's sharp ending (7:51–53) was later read by Christians as a rejection of all Jews, which it is not on Luke's own terms: Peter and Paul keep preaching to Jews throughout Acts.
views.T: The church honors Stephen as the protomartyr, with feasts on December 26 (West) and 27 (East). The fathers saw in 7:55–56 a proof that Christ is God's equal, and in Stephen's prayers the perfect martyr who forgives. Preachers, beginning with a sermon credited to Augustine, linked his prayer for his killers to Paul's later conversion. The finding of his relics in 415 spread his cult across the Christian world.

deep.h: Stephen's speech and the Old Testament: the differences
deep.b:
Stephen retells Genesis and Exodus mostly in their Greek form. In these places, the main ones, what he says differs from the Hebrew text that most English Old Testaments translate. This site's notes on each verse give the readings in full.

  • 7:2–4: where God called Abraham. Genesis 12:1 follows the move to Haran; Stephen puts the call in Mesopotamia, as Genesis 15:7, Nehemiah 9:7, Philo and Josephus also do.
  • 7:4: Terah's death. By the Hebrew numbers (Genesis 11:26, 32; Genesis 12:4), Terah lived sixty years after Abraham left; the Samaritan Pentateuch gives Terah 145 years, which fits Stephen, and Philo says the same as Stephen.
  • 7:5: not a foot of land. Abraham had no land to inherit, yet Genesis 23 has him buy the field and cave at Machpelah as a grave; Stephen means he owned nothing to live on, only a burial place.
  • 7:6: four hundred years. From Genesis 15:13; Exodus 12:40 has 430.
  • 7:7: "in this place." Exodus 3:12 says "on this mountain."
  • 7:14: seventy-five persons. The Greek of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5, and a Hebrew Exodus scroll from Qumran, have seventy-five; the Masoretic Text has seventy.
  • 7:15–16: the burial at Shechem. Genesis has Abraham buy the cave at Hebron from Ephron (Genesis 23) and Jacob buy land at Shechem from Hamor's sons (Genesis 33:19), with Jacob buried at Hebron (Genesis 50:13) and Joseph at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). Stephen joins them.
  • 7:22: Moses' education and eloquence. Not in Exodus; Exodus 4:10 has Moses call himself "heavy of mouth."
  • 7:23, 30: Moses' forties. Exodus gives only eighty and 120 (Exodus 7:7; Deuteronomy 34:7); the three forties are traditional.
  • 7:29: why Moses fled. Stephen has Moses run at the Israelite's remark; Exodus 2:15 says he ran when Pharaoh looked for a way to kill him. Exodus 2:14 has both: Moses was afraid when he heard the remark.
  • 7:30: Sinai and the angel. Exodus 3:1 says Horeb.
  • 7:32: Moses trembles. Exodus 3:6 says Moses covered his face, afraid to gaze at God; Stephen says he shook and did not dare look closely.
  • 7:42–43: Amos. The Greek of Amos 5:25–27 has Moloch and Rephan where the Hebrew has Sikkuth and Kiyyun; Stephen also says "beyond Babylon" where Amos says "beyond Damascus."
  • 7:53: angels at Sinai. Not in Exodus; drawn from the Greek of Deuteronomy 33:2 and Jewish tradition.

How to read these: Some see them as errors, by Stephen or by Luke. Many note that most come from known forms of the text and from Jewish traditions of the time, so Stephen was quoting the Bible as his hearers knew it. Some see deliberate retelling, compressing events to make a point, as Jewish retellings of Scripture often did. Luke did not smooth these differences away; he kept the speech as he received or composed it.

The Greek historian Thucydides said that where he could not recall a speech exactly, he wrote what the speaker would likely have said, "keeping as close as possible to the general sense" (History 1.22). Ancient historians generally composed speeches in this way. Readers of Acts take three positions on Stephen's speech:

  • Luke's composition, written to explain the break between the church and the temple and to prepare for the Gentile mission (Haenchen, Pervo).
  • A source from the Hellenists, reworked by Luke, which explains its distinctive views and Septuagint text (Simon, Hengel, Scharlemann).
  • A summary of what Stephen said, perhaps passed on by Paul, who heard it (Bruce, Keener in part).

The speech does not sound like Luke's other speeches: it has almost no reference to Jesus until its last lines and an unusual view of the temple, which many take as a sign that Luke drew on older material.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Stephen answers with "this place"
deep.b: The charge against Stephen turns on one phrase: he speaks against "the holy place" and says Jesus will tear down "this place" (6:13–14). My suggestion is that Stephen's speech answers by tracing the word "place" (Greek topos) through Israel's story. God promised that Israel would serve him "in this place" (7:7); at the bush "the spot (topos) you are standing on is holy ground" (7:33); and the speech ends with God asking "what place could be my place of rest?" (7:49). The "place" that matters, Stephen implies, is wherever God chooses to meet his people, from a desert bush to the right hand of God where Stephen sees Jesus standing. Commentators often discuss the temple theme; I have not seen the three uses of topos treated as the speech's backbone.

echoes: Genesis 11:26–12:5; Genesis 15:13–14; Genesis 23:16–20; Genesis 33:19; Genesis 37–50; Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1–3; Exodus 32:1–6; Exodus 33:3; Deuteronomy 18:15; Deuteronomy 33:2; Joshua 24:32; 2 Samuel 7:1–16; 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 132:5; Isaiah 66:1–2; Amos 5:25–27; Nehemiah 9:6–37; Daniel 7:13–14; Matthew 23:29–37; Luke 22:69; Luke 23:34; Luke 23:46; Hebrews 11; 22:20

settings.by: Stephen, one of the Seven, a Greek-speaking Jewish believer
settings.to: the high priest and the Sanhedrin, with his accusers and the false witnesses present
settings.when: on trial, after the high priest asks whether the charges of speaking against the temple and the law are true
settings.why: to answer the charges by retelling Israel's story: God met his people far from the land and the temple, Israel always resisted the deliverers God sent, and God cannot be housed in a building; and then to turn the charge back on his judges, who received the law and did not keep it and who killed the Righteous One
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the speech explained why faith in Jesus did not depend on the temple, and why the gospel went out from Jerusalem to the nations, while showing that this was Israel's own story, not a new religion. If Acts was written after the temple fell in AD 70, as most scholars think, the speech also helped them make sense of that loss; if it was written about 62, it read as a warning.
views: Stephen answers the charges point by point and shows he honors Moses and the law.
Stephen does not defend himself but, like the prophets, accuses Israel's leaders of repeating their ancestors' sins.

settings.when: as the council rages at the end of his speech
settings.why: to testify that the Jesus they condemned stands at God's right hand, the claim Jesus made at his own trial (Luke 22:69); it confirms the charge of blasphemy in their eyes
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that the one they worshiped was alive and standing with his witnesses in their trials.

settings.to: the Lord Jesus, in the hearing of his killers and of Saul
settings.when: while he is being stoned outside the city
settings.why: to commit his spirit to Jesus and to ask that his killers not be held guilty, as Jesus had prayed for his
settings.readers: For Luke's churches, facing persecution, Stephen was the model of a martyr's death: trusting Jesus and forgiving enemies. Among those forgiven, as the next chapters show, was Saul.

traditions.q: Stephen prays to Jesus himself: "Lord Jesus, welcome my spirit" (7:59). Should Christians pray to Jesus, or only to the Father through him?
views: Christians pray to the Father, and also to Jesus directly; prayer to Jesus, calling on his name, is an ancient and central form of Christian prayer (Catechism 2665–2668).
Yes. The Jesus Prayer, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me," is at the heart of Orthodox devotion, and Stephen's prayer is one of its roots.

Worship and prayer are given to God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and to him alone; ordinarily prayer is made to the Father in the name of the Son by the help of the Spirit (Westminster Confession 21.2–3). The Confession does not take up Stephen's case; Calvin, commenting on this verse, takes Stephen's prayer as showing that Christ may rightly be called on.
Jesus is the name of the one God, so prayer to Jesus is prayer to God himself.
Prayer is to be addressed to Jehovah alone, in Jesus' name. Witness publications explain Stephen's words as an appeal to the Jesus he saw in vision, not a pattern for prayer.
